pandemia-soledad.title: The Loneliness Pandemic
content: We can talk to almost anyone, at almost any moment. We can see what our friends are doing, meet new people, and stay in touch with someone halfway across the world. So why does loneliness still feel so familiar?

I think we've started confusing being connected with having someone beside us. Talking to people every day doesn't necessarily mean having meaningful relationships. You can receive dozens of messages and still feel there's no one you can tell what is really weighing on you.
The illusion of closeness

Social media lets us watch other people's lives without truly being part of them. We know where they went, what they ate, and who they spent time with, but sometimes have no idea how they're doing. We keep up with people we barely speak to anymore.
And I don't think phones are entirely to blame. We live in a world that seems to demand we stay busy—producing, studying, working. Friendship takes time, and too often we treat that time as a luxury.
Being alone isn't the same as feeling lonely
There's nothing wrong with enjoying your own company. The problem begins when distance from others stops being a choice.

Maybe we need fewer conversations out of obligation and more places where we can connect without having to prove anything. I don't think we necessarily need more people in our lives. Sometimes we just need to feel genuinely close to the ones already there.
Because being surrounded by people has never guaranteed that we'll feel less alone.

no-son-tus-ideas.title: These Aren’t Your Ideas
content: We like to believe our opinions belong entirely to us. That we reached them by watching the world, questioning it, and drawing our own conclusions. But how much of what we think did we really choose?
Every day we consume content selected by platforms that know our tastes, our habits, and what will keep our eyes on a screen. What we see is hardly a neutral picture of the world.
No one has to tell you what to think
Manipulation doesn't always mean forcing someone to believe something. Sometimes all it takes is showing them the same idea over and over, while every other perspective quietly disappears.

If everything you see confirms what you already believe, you may start to think everyone feels the same way. And when someone disagrees, instead of trying to understand them, you dismiss them as ignorant.

What worries me is that we can end up defending ideas we've never really stopped to question. We repeat them because we've heard them enough times, because someone we admire said them, or because thousands of people applauded them online.
Thinking critically also means doubting yourself
I'm not saying every opinion we hold is wrong. I'm saying we should ask ourselves more often where it came from.
Why do I believe this? What would it take for me to change my mind? Have I ever truly listened to someone who sees things differently?
Maybe critical thinking isn't about constantly questioning everyone else. Maybe it's about being willing to question even the things we're absolutely certain of.
Because expressing an opinion confidently doesn't mean you arrived at it on your own.

scroll-infinito.title: Endless Scrolling, Real Emptiness
content: You open an app intending to watch something for five minutes. When you check the time again, almost an hour has passed. You can't remember most of what you watched, yet your thumb keeps scrolling.
It's strange how something can take up so much of our time and leave us feeling as though we've done nothing at all.
Entertainment without an ending

Entertainment used to have a stopping point. A movie ended, an episode finished, or we closed a book. Now we can consume content for hours without ever reaching a moment when the app tells us we've had enough.
And that's no accident. Platforms compete for our attention. The longer we stay, the more chances they have to show us ads and keep us consuming.

We're constantly told it's a matter of personal responsibility: put your phone down, manage your time, have more discipline. But it seems absurd to ignore that many of these apps are designed precisely to make leaving difficult.
Are we really choosing?

I think one of the most unsettling consequences is how accustomed we've become to entertainment that arrives without us asking for it. We don't even have to decide what we want to watch anymore. The content appears, and we simply react.

This isn't about getting rid of social media or pretending all entertainment is a waste of time. It's about recognizing the moment we stop using these platforms because we want to and start using them out of habit.
Maybe the question isn't how many hours we spend on our phones, but how many of those hours we actually chose to spend there.

modelos-politicos.title: Political Models
content: We're taught to argue about political systems as if they were rival football teams. Capitalism versus socialism, left versus right, good versus bad. Yet those arguments often overlook what should matter most: how people actually live.
I find it hard to take a conversation about freedom seriously when it ignores the material conditions that make freedom possible.
Freedom has a price, too
We say everyone has opportunities, but we don't all start from the same place. Studying with time, stability, and resources is not the same as studying while working to help support your household.
And talking about the freedom to choose a job is very different when you can turn down a bad offer than when you have to accept almost anything to pay the rent.
Inequality isn't just about how much money someone has. It shapes how much time we have, which choices are available to us, and how vulnerable we are when something goes wrong.
Beyond the labels

I think we romanticize economic models too easily. Some people defend a system as if all its problems were individual mistakes. Others imagine that simply changing its name would make injustice disappear.

But no political label should matter more than the lives of the people living under it. If a society requires millions to live in constant fear of getting sick, losing their job, or being unable to afford a home, something deserves to be questioned.
I'm not interested in defending a model just because it sounds good in theory. I want to know who it works for, and who ends up paying the price.
We can argue for hours about which system is superior. But if we leave out the people living within it, perhaps we're arguing about the least important part.

peso-de-estar-informado.title: The Weight of Being Informed
content: You open social media and see a war, a natural disaster, an economic crisis, or news that someone has just died. You scroll and find another tragedy. Then another. And another.
There was a time when staying informed meant going out of your way to find the news. Now the news seems to follow us, even when all we want is a little distraction.
The pressure to know everything

There's a strange pressure to have an opinion about absolutely everything that happens. If you haven't heard about the latest international conflict, you seem disconnected from reality. If you step away from the news for a while, you might feel as though you simply don't care.
But do we really need to hear about every tragedy in the world, every single day?

I think we've confused being informed with being constantly exposed to information. We can spend hours reading stories that frighten, anger, or sadden us without understanding their causes any better—or knowing what to do about them.
When suffering becomes content
I also find it unsettling how quickly we move from watching someone suffer to a funny video, an advertisement, or a pointless argument. Everything is mixed together on the same screen.
A tragedy can trend for a few days and disappear as soon as a more shocking story comes along. The problem hasn't gone away; our attention has simply been redirected elsewhere.

I don't believe the answer is to ignore what happens in the world. Indifference isn't a solution either. But keeping informed should help us understand reality, not merely fill us with anxiety about things that often lie beyond our control.
Being informed matters. Living in a constant state of worry shouldn't be the price we pay for it.

concentracion.title: We Can’t Focus Anymore
content: When was the last time you did something for a whole hour without checking your phone?

I'm not just talking about studying. I mean reading a book, watching a movie, or simply sitting down without feeling the urge to do something else. Sometimes we genuinely want to focus, but our own minds seem unwilling to stay still.
The need to do something else

We can put on a film we've wanted to see for weeks and find ourselves checking social media ten minutes later. We try to study, but every notification seems more interesting than what's in front of us.
And when no notifications arrive, we go looking for distractions ourselves.

I think we've grown so used to constant stimulation that anything requiring patience starts to feel unbearably slow. We want to learn, but become frustrated when we don't understand something immediately. We want to read, but struggle to stay with a book for more than a few pages.
It's not always a lack of discipline
It's easy to blame people for struggling to focus. To call them lazy, say they lack willpower, or tell them to just put their phones away.

But there's something contradictory about demanding perfect concentration while surrounding ourselves with platforms competing to interrupt it. Our ability to focus also depends on the environment in which we're trying to do so.
I don't think we've lost our ability to pay attention forever. But I do think we're normalizing a way of living in which every moment of silence has to be filled immediately.
And that worries me, because focus isn't only useful for studying or working. It helps us listen to someone, enjoy something without rushing, and think for ourselves.
Maybe reclaiming our attention begins with accepting that we don't have to be entertained every moment of the day.

cuanto-cuesta-estar-bien.title: What Does It Cost to Be Okay?
content: How many times have we heard that our mental health should come first?
That we need more rest, exercise, therapy, time for our hobbies, and distance from whatever hurts us.
It all sounds reasonable enough. The problem is that tomorrow we still have to wake up for work, pay the rent, and find something to eat.
And none of those responsibilities disappear just because we decide to put our well-being first.
The privilege of having time
There's something contradictory about living in a society that demands constant productivity and then, when that pressure starts to wear us down, tells us the answer is to manage our time better.
As if we all had the same opportunities. As if resting were always a choice, rather than—in many cases—a privilege.

Someone who studies and works at the same time may know perfectly well that they need more sleep, better meals, or simply a few hours to themselves. But knowing what you need doesn't mean you have the freedom to do it.
And this is where I think so many conversations about mental health fall short. We talk endlessly about what people should do, and far less about the conditions they need to be able to do it.
We don't always choose what's good for us
Think of someone coming home after an exhausting day at work. They know they could use their free time to study, learn something, cook a healthier meal, or exercise.
But they get home and all they want is to lie down, order food, watch videos, or have a drink to switch off.
From the outside, it's easy to call it a discipline problem. To say they should try harder, plan better, or stop wasting time.
But maybe that person doesn't need another lesson in organizing their life. Maybe they need a life that doesn't drain every bit of energy out of them before they even get home.

That doesn't mean every escape is healthy. Alcohol, for example, can become another problem in itself. But understanding why someone looks for a quick way out of exhaustion isn't the same as excusing every choice they make.
Even rest has to be productive
I also find it strange that even self-care is marketed as a way to perform better.
Sleep well so you can be more efficient. Exercise so you have more energy for work. Meditate so you can handle stress and keep meeting your responsibilities.
When did we stop believing that feeling okay was valuable in its own right?
It seems that even when we rest, we have to find a way to justify it. As though time spent living our own lives is something we have to earn after taking care of every obligation.
It isn't just an individual responsibility

I don't think we should abandon our personal efforts. Some choices really can improve our lives, and that matters. But we can't use individual responsibility as an excuse to ignore the conditions we live under.
Not everyone can afford therapy. Not everyone can walk away from a job that's hurting them. Not everyone has a family that can help financially while they try to get back on their feet.
And it doesn't feel fair to speak about well-being as though everyone had access to the same solutions.
Maybe we should stop asking only why some people aren't taking better care of their mental health and start asking what kind of life we're demanding they live.
Because taking care of our mental health matters. But so do eating, working, studying, and paying the bills.
And a society in which survival takes all our energy deserves to be questioned before we're told to learn how to rest better.

esclavos-de-la-nostalgia.title: Prisoners of Nostalgia
content: At what point does remembering what once made us happy begin to keep us from being happy again?

There are songs we stop listening to because they remind us of someone. Photographs we can't bring ourselves to delete, and places we'd give anything to return to—not because they're extraordinary, but because we were once happy there.
Sometimes all it takes is one song to feel as though we've stepped back into a part of our lives we thought we'd left behind.
And for a few seconds, it feels beautiful.
Until we remember we're not there anymore.
The past always seems like a better place
I think we have a strange ability to remember what was beautiful and forget everything that hurt us, too.
We miss people we might not actually have been that happy with. Periods of our lives that were full of problems. Moments we probably didn't appreciate nearly as much while we were living them.
Maybe what we miss isn't what really happened, but the version of it our memories have created.
And whenever we compare that version of the past with our present, the present almost always loses.
Because we're comparing a real life, with all its difficulties, to a memory from which we've quietly erased so many imperfections.
When remembering becomes a habit
There's something strange about returning again and again to memories we know will hurt.
We play the same songs, look through the same photographs, or imagine conversations that never happened.
Sometimes we even go looking for that sadness.
Not because we enjoy suffering, but because the feeling seems like one of the few things still connecting us to what we've lost.
Little by little, we can begin confusing remembering something with keeping alive something that has already ended.
As though no longer feeling sad would mean it had never mattered.
But how long can we keep living emotionally in a place we can never return to?
Missing something can also be a way of escaping
Maybe one of the hardest parts of nostalgia is accepting that we don't always miss a person or a place.
Sometimes we miss who we were when we were there.
We miss the way we thought, the hopes we had, or the feeling that so much of life was still waiting for us.
And when the present doesn't look the way we imagined it would, the past begins to feel like a refuge.
A place we return to in our minds because we know its story, and we already know how it ends.
The problem is that we can grow so accustomed to living inside those memories that we stop noticing what's still happening right in front of us.
The life we haven't lived yet
I don't believe forgetting is the answer.
It would be absurd to try to erase the people, places, and moments that made us who we are.
And I don't think we should stop listening to certain songs or looking at photographs simply because they make us sad.
The problem begins when our happiness starts depending on bringing back something that no longer exists.

When we stop meeting new people because none of them feels like someone from our past. When we turn away from new experiences because we're convinced they'll never be as special as the ones we've already had.
And maybe the saddest thing about living this way is that we can spend years missing one chapter of our lives while overlooking another that we'll someday miss just as much.
We can't go back to the past. But we can still make memories that will one day mean every bit as much.
Perhaps the real problem with nostalgia isn't that it makes us miss what we've lived, but that it sometimes stops us from living the things we'll someday miss, too.

capital-humano.title: Human Capital
content: How much is a human life worth?

It sounds like an absurd question. A life shouldn't have a price. Yet we live in a world where our worth so often seems tied to how much money we can make, how much we can produce, and how useful we are to someone else.

Imagine a father who's spent twenty years working for the same company. For two decades he's woken up early, come home exhausted, and missed birthdays, family gatherings, and moments he'll never get back. He's done it because he has a family to feed, a home to pay for, and people depending on him.

Then one day, the company decides it needs to cut costs. His position disappears, and someone else can do the same job for less money. Twenty years of effort are reduced to an administrative decision. To the company, it's a necessary adjustment. To him, it might mean not knowing how he'll pay next month's rent.
And while the company carries on as usual, somewhere a family is sitting at home trying to work out what happens next.
That's what we so often forget when we talk about the economy. Behind every layoff, every pay cut, every decision made to maximize profits, there are people whose lives can change completely.
We talk about workers as though they're numbers. Human resources. Labor force. Human capital. Words that may help us describe an economy, but can also make us forget the lives they stand for.
A person is more than what they produce.

They're someone who might come home too tired to play with their children. Someone choosing between a doctor's appointment and groceries. Someone who's spent years enduring a job they hate because they can't afford to be without an income.
And the saddest part is that so many of these people aren't trying to get rich. They just want a little peace.

They want to make it to the end of the month without fear. To have time for their families. To get sick without worrying that their future is falling apart. They want a life that doesn't revolve entirely around the need to work.
But in a world that puts money first, even those ordinary things can begin to feel like privileges.

From childhood, we're told to study, work hard, and prepare ourselves for a good job. That if we try hard enough, we can build a stable life. But no one can promise all that effort will ever be rewarded.

You can do everything right and still lose everything. You can spend your youth building a career, only to discover years later that your skills are no longer in demand. You can give much of your life to a company and be replaced the moment it's more convenient.
And then comes a feeling that's hard to put into words: realizing you've given so much of yourself, only to learn you were far more replaceable than you ever imagined.

Capital doesn't care about individuals. It doesn't know your children's names, how hard it was to get out of bed this morning, or what it means to come home and pretend everything is fine so your family won't worry. Its logic is different: grow, compete, and produce more.

That doesn't mean everyone running a business is cruel or indifferent. It means we've built an economy in which decisions are so often made with the numbers in mind first, and the human consequences second.
And those consequences don't always show up in financial reports.

You won't find the father losing sleep because he's afraid of being fired. The mother working overtime, feeling as though her children are growing up without her. The young person giving up their dreams because the family needs money. Or the uncomfortable conversations around the kitchen table when the bills start piling up.
They're small, everyday tragedies that rarely draw attention because they've become far too common.

Sometimes we even blame ourselves for falling behind. When we're tired, we tell ourselves to get organized. When we don't earn enough, we assume we didn't work hard enough. When we lose our job, we wonder what we did wrong.
As if everything depended only on our choices, rather than on the conditions we live in, too.
This isn't about saying work doesn't matter or businesses shouldn't make money. It's about questioning why we've grown so comfortable with sacrificing people's well-being when profits are at stake.
Because behind every worker is a life that doesn't stop when their shift ends. There are people waiting at home, worries no one else knows about, and moments that will never come back.

Maybe the most painful part is how normal it all seems now. We hear that hundreds of people have lost their jobs, and we go on with our day. We see figures, percentages, and headlines about economic growth, but rarely stop to imagine the stories behind them.
And one day, any one of us could become one of those figures.
Because what is the point of building an ever-growing economy if the people holding it together have less and less time, peace of mind, and freedom to live?
Progress shouldn't be measured only by how much money we can generate, but by how many lives we can make better.
Because a human life should be worth so much more than what it can produce.

vale-la-pena-ser-reemplazados-por-la-ia.title: Is It Worth Being Replaced by AI?
content: We live in a time when technology moves faster than we can fully understand. Every year brings tools that do things that seemed impossible not long ago. Artificial intelligence can write, code, design, and finish in seconds work that used to take people hours.
And as fascinating as all those possibilities are, there's a question I can't seem to shake.
Are we really moving forward as a society, or are we simply finding new ways to produce more while spending less?

I'm not against artificial intelligence. Denying what it could do would be absurd. It could shorten working hours, take over dangerous jobs, improve medicine, and give people more time to actually live.
But something worries me far more than the technology itself: the hands we're placing its future in.
Because while we talk about intelligent machines and an automated world, millions of people are still working under conditions that should have disappeared decades ago.

Some workers spend almost their entire day away from home and still don't earn enough to live with any peace of mind. Others have no paid leave, social security, or basic employment benefits. Families depend on informal work, where getting sick can mean losing the income they need to survive.
And meanwhile, we're told the future will be wonderful because companies will be able to do the same work with fewer employees.
Wonderful for whom?
Sometimes it feels as though we're more concerned with building machines that can work like people than with making sure people can work with dignity.
And the saddest part is that we don't even need to imagine some dystopian future to find examples of this.
Think of something as ordinary as a chocolate bar.
For many of us, it's just something we pick up at a store. Cheap, sweet, and entirely unremarkable. But behind the cocoa used to make it lies a reality we rarely see.

In Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire, two of the world's leading cocoa producers, child labor remains a serious problem. A study published in 2020, using data from 2018 and 2019, estimated that around 1.56 million children were involved in child labor in cocoa production in the areas it studied.

We're not simply talking about children occasionally helping their families. Many carry out dangerous tasks, use tools that can injure them, and work under conditions that put their health and education at risk.
While a child works on a plantation, someone somewhere else in the world enjoys the finished product without knowing its story.

I'm not saying this to blame anyone for buying chocolate. I'm saying it because it's hard to make sense of how we've built supply chains so enormous that we can enjoy their rewards without ever having to look directly at the suffering behind them.

Cocoa is grown in West Africa, but a significant share of the value generated by the chocolate industry is captured farther along the chain—in manufacturing, marketing, and the sale of finished products. Many farming families receive only a small share of the final price.
The people doing some of the hardest work aren't necessarily the ones who benefit most from it.
That's a contradiction worth sitting with.
We have the technology to build increasingly complex systems, yet we still haven't ensured fair conditions for millions of workers.
So if a company can make enormous profits while keeping labor costs low, what incentive does it have to change that model voluntarily?
Why would it spend more on wages, safety, and well-being if it can continue making money without doing so?
And this is where artificial intelligence starts to worry me.
Not because machines are evil, or because replacing certain human tasks is necessarily wrong. There are dangerous, repetitive, exhausting jobs we'd be better off leaving behind.
The problem is that getting rid of a job doesn't automatically make life better for the person who used to do it.

Imagine someone who's spent fifteen years working to support their family. Maybe they don't particularly like the job. Maybe they come home tired every day and barely have time to be with their children.
One day, they learn the company is introducing an AI system that can handle much of their work.
For the company, it might mean lower costs and higher productivity.
For that person, it could mean losing the income their entire family depends on.
And suddenly there are two very different ways of describing the same breakthrough.
One speaks of efficiency, innovation, and growth. The other speaks of uncertainty, fear, and not knowing what tomorrow will bring.
It's worth remembering that not every job will disappear. The International Labour Organization has argued that generative AI is more likely to transform many jobs than replace them outright.
But even if most people keep their jobs, that still leaves one fundamental question unanswered.
Who gets to enjoy the benefits of that transformation?
If a tool allows someone to do in four hours what once took eight, we could use it to shorten the working day without cutting their pay.
We could give them more time to rest, study, spend time with their family, or simply do things they enjoy.
But there's another possibility: demand twice as much output in the same eight hours, cut staff, and increase profits.
Technology makes both possible. A machine doesn't make that decision.
And when we look at the inequalities that already exist at work, it's hard to blindly trust that those benefits will be shared fairly.

We also can't ignore the imbalance of power. Someone who loses their job may spend months wondering how to pay the bills, while a large company has resources, advisers, and opportunities that person can barely imagine accessing.

Companies can face penalties, and labor laws exist to protect workers. But having rights on paper doesn't always mean being able to exercise them. In many places, demanding fair treatment can mean risking the only income you have.
Sometimes we talk about changing jobs as if everyone had that freedom.
As if a mother could leave her job without thinking about how she'll feed her children. As if someone in debt could turn down a miserable wage simply because they know they deserve better.
Not everyone can afford to choose.
And perhaps that's what saddens me most about this whole conversation.
We get excited imagining smart cities, robots, and systems capable of doing almost anything. We picture a future where machines do all the work for us.
But we rarely stop to think about those who can't even enjoy the most basic conditions of the present.

What's the point of celebrating a new technological revolution while children are still working on plantations, adults are growing old in exhausting jobs, and families live in fear of losing their only source of income?
I don't think we should stop developing artificial intelligence. Technology can improve our lives, too, and it would be unfair to overlook everything good it might bring.
But we shouldn't confuse technological advancement with human progress.
A society doesn't necessarily become better just because its companies produce more, its machines get smarter, or its products become cheaper.
We should also care about how much rest workers get, how secure their families feel, and how many people can live without fearing that one financial setback could destroy everything they've built.
And when we talk about child labor, exploitation, or unfair working conditions, we shouldn't treat them as unavoidable sacrifices required to keep the economy running.
If a system depends on some people living badly so others can reap greater rewards, then the way that system is organized deserves to be questioned.
Maybe one day AI really will free us from work nobody wants to do. Maybe it will let us live more peacefully and spend our time on the things that matter to us.
I'd like to believe that future is possible.
But I also worry we'll end up building a world where machines do more and more, while people have less and less control over their own lives.
Because in the end, the question shouldn't be only whether artificial intelligence can replace us.
We should be asking why we've become so willing to accept that a person's worth depends on how profitable it is to keep them around.
And above all, whether the future we're building is really meant to make our lives better—or simply to increase the profits of those who already have more than enough.
